source.title: Coherent Gradients: An Approach to Understanding Generalization in Gradient Descent-based Optimization

record.file_problem: Full paper text supplied; no apparent truncation or garbling that prevents extraction.
record.tranche_reason: The paper tests random and partially randomized labels on MNIST and reports training and test accuracy and learning dynamics. It uses a different small fully connected network and setup from the cited originals, so this is a conceptual reproduction.
record.gate_note: The paper also discusses cited results on random labels, but those are not recorded as this study’s results. Rows below cover its own label-noise experiment. Winsorized-SGD results are not rows because that intervention is outside the claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study independently tests random-label fitting and learning dynamics using a fixed MNIST network and vanilla SGD across five label-noise levels.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly accurate. The authors propose coherent gradients as a mechanism favoring changes that benefit many examples, present heuristic and experimental support, and show that suppressing weak gradient directions reduces overfitting. They describe the 75% aggregate-contribution evidence as weaker and qualify the sampled per-example contribution analysis more generally.
record.recipe_differences: Tests the random-label memorization and learning dynamics on MNIST using a one-hidden-layer fully connected network, vanilla SGD, and a sweep of randomized-label proportions; the paper states that the cited originals are being replicated, but its setup is a simple baseline rather than a direct same-recipe reproduction.
record.method_sensitivity: Label-noise fraction changes the time to reach a given accuracy and pristine/corrupt contribution patterns; the 75% noise comparison is weaker.
record.problems: Only one dataset and a simple fully connected architecture are tested. Exact curve values are largely figure-based; the pristine/corrupt gradient analysis samples 400 examples and 600 weights, and the authors describe the 75% noise evidence as weaker and not overwhelmingly significant.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted from the label-noise results. Figure 4 concerns winsorized SGD, a modified optimizer intervention not covered by the listed claim versions, so it is mentioned in gate_note rather than extracted as a claim row.

untested.parts: This study's chance-level test performance cannot be verified from the supplied figure text.
The small constant-factor increase in time to fit random versus true labels is not quantified.
No shuffled-pixel, independently permuted-pixel, or Gaussian-noise input experiments.
The steady test-error progression toward chance cannot be established from the supplied text.
No comparisons with weight decay, dropout, or augmentation; no direct removal ablation testing their effects on true-label generalization.

missing.what: Good true-label generalization without explicit regularizers: the clean MNIST baseline generalizes well despite the absence of regularization. Add a baseline test-performance row, retaining the qualitative value if numerical curves remain unavailable.
Pristine-example learning slows as their proportion decreases. This directly qualifies the speed of clean-pattern acquisition while preserving the reported pristine-before-corrupt ordering.
Figure 3 reports mean cumulative per-example loss-reduction contributions for 25% and 50% noise as well as 75%. R10 captures only the latter and omits the direction of the comparison.

record.verdict_notes: Unavailable numerical ratios and unreadable figure curves are evidence gaps, not scope-limiting results. The 75% aggregate-gradient crossover is affected by group sizes and does not establish a failure of real-label-first learning. Winsorized-SGD experiments were explicitly declared omitted; they do not directly test V5's named regularizers.

versions.untested_parts: Tests fully random labels on MNIST with a one-hidden-layer fully connected network; does not test other datasets, architectures, or optimizers.
Reports qualitative slowing as label noise increases, but does not quantify a small constant factor in training time.
Tests five noise levels (0%, 25%, 50%, 75%, 100%) and training accuracy, test accuracy and learning dynamics; does not report a steadily rising numerical test-error sequence.
Compares learning rates of pristine and corrupt examples in mixed-noise datasets; does not test the full claim across noisy and completely random labels over training.

rows.subject: fully connected network with one hidden layer of 2048 ReLUs and a 10-way softmax
rows.operation_detail: Tracked first training step when pristine and corrupt examples were learned under mixed label noise.
rows.measure: Relative learning rate / first training step when an example is learned, separated by pristine versus corrupt labels
rows.value: Pristine examples are learned faster than corrupt examples; pristine learning is closer to the 0% noise rate and corrupt learning closer to the 100% noise rate.
rows.note: The paper reports the group-level comparison and describes the plotted first-learning-step curves.
rows.check: Pristine means labels actually unchanged, including examples whose labels remained correct after permutation. These groups are not identical to examples selected versus unselected for randomization.

rows.subject: fully connected network with one hidden layer of 2048 ReLUs and a 10-way softmax
rows.operation_detail: Estimated relative contributions of pristine and corrupt examples to point-in-time loss reduction from sampled per-example gradients.
rows.measure: Fractions of loss reduction attributed to pristine and corrupt examples (ftp and ftc)
rows.baseline: Null simulations with randomly permuted pristine/corrupt designations
rows.value: For 25% label noise, ftp initially starts off higher than ftc and after a few steps they cross over; the null curves do not cross over.
rows.note: The authors say this increases confidence that the null may be rejected.
rows.check: This measures estimated contributions to training-loss reduction, providing supplementary learning-dynamics evidence rather than directly measuring first learning.

rows.measure: Fractions of loss reduction attributed to pristine and corrupt examples (ftp and ftc)
rows.baseline: Null simulations with randomly permuted pristine/corrupt designations
rows.value: The crossover does not happen; there is a slight slope downwards for the contribution from pristine examples.
rows.note: Authors say the 75% case is weaker; nulls also show corrupt greater than pristine, attributed to differing set sizes.
rows.check: The weak downward trend supplies limited supplementary evidence. Lack of crossover in aggregate contributions is confounded by unequal group sizes and does not show that pristine examples cease to be learned first.

rows.operation_detail: Compared mean cumulative contributions of pristine and corrupt examples during the first 10 training steps.

rows.value: The results appear somewhat significant but not overwhelmingly so.
rows.note: The authors say it would be interesting to redo this on the entire population of examples and trainable parameters instead of a small sample.
rows.check: The recorded value describes evidential strength without stating which group contributes more. Figure 3 covers all three mixed-noise conditions, and the prose's significance qualification is not explicitly restricted to 75% noise.
